title: Finite torsion-free modules over a domain embed into finite free modules
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain and let $M$ be a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Suppose $M$ is torsion free, meaning that $am=0$ with $0\ne a\in R$ implies $m=0$. Then there exist an integer $r\geq0$ and an injective $R$-linear map $i:M\to R^r$, where $R^r$ is the module of $r$-tuples with coordinatewise operations, including $R^0=0$.

source.place: Tag 0AUU (more-algebra-lemma-finite-torsion-free-submodule-free), torsion-free implies finite-free embedding; more-algebra.tex:4863-4884.

proof.text: Put $S=R\setminus\{0\}$, a multiplicative subset since $R$ is a domain, and form $K=S^{-1}R$ and $V=S^{-1}M$ by [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. For $M=R$ the fraction operations give the ring $K$: $(a/s)(b/t)=ab/(st)$ and $1=1/1$. The fraction equality criterion and cancellation in $R$ show $a/s=0$ exactly when $a=0$, hence $R\to K$, $a\mapsto a/1$, is injective and $1\ne0$ in $K$. Each nonzero $a/s$ has inverse $s/a$, so $K$ is a field and $V$ is a $K$-vector space.

Let $j:M\to V$ be $m\mapsto m/1$. The kernel criterion in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] says $j(m)=0$ implies $um=0$ for some $u\in S$. Torsion freeness gives $m=0$, so $j$ is injective. Choose generators $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ by [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. If $m=\sum_i c_i x_i$ with $c_i\in R$, then $m/s=\sum_i(c_i/s)j(x_i)$. Thus the finitely many $j(x_i)$ span $V$ over $K$.

By [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free], choose a basis $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}$ of $V$. In the finite-support expansions of $j(x_1),\ldots,j(x_n)$ in this basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module], let $J\subseteq I$ be the union of their supports. It is finite. Every vector of $V$ is a linear combination of the $j(x_i)$ and therefore has zero basis coefficients outside $J$. If $\alpha\in I\setminus J$, the vector $e_\alpha$ would have coefficient both $1$ and $0$ at $\alpha$, contradicting uniqueness of basis expansions. Hence $I=J$ is finite. Enumerate the basis as $e_1,\ldots,e_r$; unique expansion defines the $K$-linear coordinate isomorphism $\theta:V\xrightarrow{\sim}K^r$.

Write $	heta(j(x_i))_k=a_{ik}/b_{ik}$ with $a_{ik}\in R$ and $b_{ik}\in S$ for $1\le i\le n$, $1\le k\le r$. Put $b=\prod_{i,k}b_{ik}
e0$ (the empty product is $1$). Then $b\,a_{ik}/b_{ik}=a_{ik}\prod_{(h,l)
e(i,k)}b_{hl}$ lies in the embedded copy of $R\subset K$. For $m=\sum_i c_i x_i$, each coordinate of $b	heta(j(m))$ equals $\sum_i c_i a_{ik}\prod_{(h,l)
e(i,k)}b_{hl}\in R$. This is independent of the chosen expression for $m$, since it is the coordinate of the fixed vector $b	heta(j(m))$ and $R	o K$ is injective.

Define $i:M\to R^r$ by taking these unique $R$-valued coordinates of $b\theta(j(m))$. Additivity and $R$-linearity follow coordinatewise from those of $j$ and $\theta$ and injectivity of $R\to K$. If $i(m)=0$, then $b\theta(j(m))=0$ in $K^r$. As $b\ne0$, it is invertible in $K$; thus $\theta(j(m))=0$, then $j(m)=0$, and finally $m=0$. This proves injectivity. For $r=0$ the same argument shows $V=0$ and $M=0$, giving the required map to $R^0=0$.
